pattern_id: Crash-induced SafetyRules lock amnesia enabling conflicting HotStuff commits
description: In Aptos HotStuff-style consensus, SafetyRules tracks a lock on branches via SafetyData fields such as last_voted_round, preferred_round, and one_chain_round. Under a crash-window persistence bug, the durable SafetyData can lag behind the validator's true in-memory state, so that after restart the node reloads a weaker lock than it actually held before crashing. The test `crash_induced_lock_amnesia_cannot_enable_conflicting_commits` in `consensus/safety-rules` models a single honest-but-crashable validator H2 that votes along a 3-chain X1<-X2<-X3 before crashing, establishing a lock on branch X. We then reinitialize SafetyRules from a manually regressed SafetyData that only records last_voted_round up to r1 and resets preferred_round/one_chain_round, approximating lock amnesia. After restart, a conflicting 3-chain Y1<-Y2<-Y3 is presented on a different branch. Due to relying solely on the regressed SafetyData, current SafetyRules accepts a new vote for Y3 at the same round r3, even though H2 previously voted for X3. By embedding these votes into an n=4, f=1 configuration with one Byzantine validator, an attacker can form two conflicting QCs (for X3 and Y3) with overlapping honest voters, which can be extended to conflicting commits in a full HotStuff deployment. The bug violates the safety invariant that an honest validator must never support two conflicting 3-chains at equal or higher rounds, even across crashes.
trigger_condition: A validator first votes along a 3-chain on branch X (establishing a strong lock), then crashes in a window where its in-memory SafetyData has been updated but the durable storage still reflects only an older, weaker lock. After restart SafetyRules is reconstructed from this stale SafetyData, and the validator is presented with a conflicting 3-chain on branch Y at the same or a higher round. Because lock/preferred_round are read only from the regressed SafetyData without cross-checking against prior votes or stronger locks, SafetyRules permits a vote on Y, enabling two conflicting QCs and potentially conflicting commits.
test_template:
1) Model a single honest-but-crashable validator V as a one-validator epoch using the protocol's SafetyRules equivalent.
2) Construct a 3-chain (or the protocol's minimum commit chain) on branch X (e.g., X1<-X2<-X3) and have V vote on all blocks, capturing the true post-vote SafetyData.
3) Emulate a crash by reinitializing SafetyRules from a manually regressed SafetyData that only records a weaker lock (e.g., last_voted_round <= r1 and lower preferred_round/one_chain_round), omitting the latest votes.
4) After restart, build a conflicting 3-chain Y1<-Y2<-Y3 that shares the same ancestor height but is not on the X branch, and request a vote for Y3 (optionally using timeout certificates or alternative QCs if the protocol allows TC-based justification).
5) If a new vote for Y3 is produced and its block id differs from the pre-crash X3 vote, embed the resulting votes into an n=3f+1 validator set with at most f Byzantine validators and construct two conflicting QCs or commit certificates whose signer sets intersect in at least one honest validator. An assertion that this occurs indicates a safety violation due to crash-induced lock amnesia.
